title: The Masnavi begins
hookLine: his student Husam al-Din asks for a book, and Rumi dictates about 25,000 couplets in six books

cards: Ever had a friend ask you for something that changed your life? Can you help me move. Will you coach the team.
You should really write that down. Most of the time you say yes and forget. Sometimes the yes lasts years.

Around 1258 in Konya, a devoted student of Rumi's named Husam al-Din came to him with a request. You've written thousands of short poems, he said. Your students love the long teaching poems of the older Sufi masters.
Write us a book like that. Rumi said yes, and kept at it, on and off, for about fifteen years. Today's word is masnavi.

teach.b: Masnavi is first the name of a form.
In Persian poetry, a masnavi is a long poem in rhyming couplets: each pair of lines rhymes with itself, then the next pair takes a new rhyme, so a poem can run as long as a story needs.
The word comes from an Arabic root meaning two, or in pairs. Poets before Rumi, like Sanai and Attar, had used the form for great teaching poems, and those were the books Husam had in mind.
Rumi's became so well-known that people often just call it the Masnavi, as if there were no other.

A story people tell: when Husam asked, Rumi reached into his turban and pulled out a paper with the first eighteen lines already written. Charming, and probably legend. Better attested is how the rest was made.
Rumi spoke it aloud, often at night, sometimes while walking or listening to music, and Husam wrote it down and read it back so Rumi could correct it.
After the first book came a pause of about two years, when Husam's wife died. Then it went on.
Six books. Around twenty-five thousand couplets. Stories of kings and grocers, lions and parrots, woven with verses of the Qur'an and teaching about the soul.
The sixth book breaks off unfinished; Rumi died in 1273. This camp will read from it for months, story by story, so today is page one.
The long book begins not with genius, but with a friend asking, and someone saying yes.

how: The Masnavi is read aloud and taught in study circles in Iran, Afghanistan, Turkey and South Asia, often a few couplets at a time with a teacher's commentary, and the Mevlevi tradition gives it a central place.

games.q: you're Husam al-Din. your teacher has written thousands of short poems, and his students want more. what do you do?
o: collect the short poems into one book.
ask him for a long teaching poem.
games.why: Husam asked for a long book like Sanai's and Attar's. Rumi said yes, and kept at it, on and off, for about fifteen years.

practice: Think of something long that's been waiting for you: a big book, a language, a garden, a letter your kids will read when they're older.
Don't plan the whole thing; just picture the first page, the first row, the first line, and decide what that first small step is, and when.

wordCard.voice: Masnavi. A long Persian poem in rhyming couplets, and the name of Rumi's great six-book work. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: in pairs. a poem in rhyming couplets.

carryVoice: Your line: begin the long book. Every long book has a page one. Day one hundred sixty-two, done.
